label: Rank, nullity, Sylvester and Frobenius — mastery test (unseen)

items.explanation: Successive rows differ by the constant vector (1,1,0,0), so the rows are in arithmetic progression and every row lies in span{R1, (1,1,0,0)} — a two-dimensional space. The columns confirm it: C3 = 2C4 and C2 − C1 = C3. This is June 2026 Q26.
items.check: The determinant is 0, so the rank is below 4; and R1 is not a multiple of any other row, so it is above 1.

items.stem: The rank of [[1, 2], [2, 4]] is:
items.explanation: The second row is exactly twice the first, so there is only one independent row. Equivalently the determinant 1·4 − 2·2 = 0 rules out full rank, and the matrix is non-zero so the rank is not 0.
items.check: A 2 × 2 matrix has rank 0, 1 or 2 only; zero determinant with a non-zero entry forces rank 1.

items.stem: The rank of the n × n matrix all of whose entries are 1 is:
items.explanation: Every row is the same vector (1, 1, …, 1), so the row space is one-dimensional. Its nullity is therefore n − 1, which is option C — the null space is every vector whose entries sum to zero.
items.check: Verified at n = 3, 5 and 8: rank 1 in every case. The matrix is non-zero so the rank is at least 1, and all rows being identical caps it at 1.

items.stem: If a 5 × 5 matrix has rank 5, then its determinant is:
items.explanation: Full rank for a square matrix is equivalent to non-singularity, which is equivalent to a non-zero determinant and to the existence of an inverse. The nullity is then 0.

items.stem: Elementary row operations change the rank of a matrix:
options: only if a row is scaled
items.explanation: Row swaps, scaling by a non-zero constant and adding a multiple of one row to another all leave the row space unchanged, so they leave its dimension unchanged. This is precisely why row reduction is a valid method for finding a rank.

items.stem: For a matrix A of order 3 × 5, the rank is at most:
items.explanation: The rank cannot exceed either dimension, so it is capped by min(3, 5) = 3. If it attains 3, the nullity is 5 − 3 = 2, since rank–nullity uses the number of columns.
items.check: Five columns cannot be independent in a space of dimension 3, so there must be at least two independent solutions of Ax = 0.

items.stem: Let A and B be two square matrices of order n × n and let υ(·) denote nullity. Then:
options: max{υ(A), υ(B)} ≤ υ(AB) ≤ υ(A) + υ(B) − n
items.explanation: This is Sylvester's rank inequality rewritten with υ = n − rank: the upper rank bound min{rank A, rank B} becomes the lower nullity bound max{υ(A), υ(B)}, and the lower rank bound rank A + rank B − n becomes the upper nullity bound υ(A) + υ(B). June 2026 Q1. Option A's extra −n fails at once for A = B = I, where it claims 0 ≤ −n.
The rank is 2, from the arithmetic progression in the rows, and the matrix has 4 columns, so rank–nullity gives υ = 4 − 2 = 2.
items.check: Rank–nullity uses the COLUMN count. Here the matrix is square so rows and columns agree, but the habit matters for rectangular matrices.

items.stem: The rank of a matrix whose rows form an arithmetic progression — each row equal to the previous plus a fixed vector — is at most:
items.explanation: Row k equals R1 + (k−1)d, so every row lies in span{R1, d}, a space of dimension at most 2. The size of the matrix is irrelevant: a 100 × 100 matrix with this structure still has rank at most 2. This is the general principle behind June 2026 Q26.
items.check: Verified for 4 × 4, 5 × 5 and 6 × 6 matrices built this way from random R1 and d: rank 2 in every case.

items.stem: The rank of a non-zero skew-symmetric matrix is:
items.explanation: The non-zero eigenvalues of a skew-symmetric matrix occur in conjugate imaginary pairs ±iλ, so there is an even number of them. A non-zero 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrix therefore has rank exactly 2, and nullity 1. Checked over several thousand random skew-symmetric matrices of orders 2 to 6: every non-zero rank observed was 2, 4 or 6.

items.stem: If the rank of an n × n matrix is n − 1, its nullity is:
items.explanation: Rank–nullity gives υ = n − (n − 1) = 1. The matrix is singular with a one-dimensional null space, so Ax = 0 has a one-parameter family of solutions and Ax = b has either none or a one-parameter family.
items.check: Nullity 0 would mean non-singular, which contradicts a rank below n.

items.stem: The rank of the centring matrix I − (1/n)11ᵀ is:
items.explanation: The matrix is idempotent, so its rank equals its trace, which is n − (1/n)·n = n − 1. Its nullity is 1: it annihilates exactly the constant vectors. Verified at n = 4, 6 and 10 — rank n − 1, trace n − 1, idempotent in each case.
items.check: Centring removes one degree of freedom, the overall mean, which is why the rank drops by exactly 1.

items.stem: Consider the rank of the matrices a linear model is built from.
items.explanation: A is the idempotent identity, which is how all these ranks are found. B is true: the centring matrix is idempotent with trace n − 1. C is true for every real matrix. D is false — the nullity of the residual maker is k and its RANK is n − k, which is the standard slip.
statements: If A is idempotent of order n, then rank(A) = trace(A).
The centring matrix I − (1/n)11ᵀ has rank n − 1 and nullity 1.
rank(AᵀA) = rank(A) for every real matrix A.
For X of order n × k with rank k, the nullity of I − X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is n − k.

A.why: True. Idempotence forces every eigenvalue to be 0 or 1; the rank counts the ones and the trace sums them. It needs idempotence — the Q26 matrix has trace 15 and rank 2.

B.why: True. It is idempotent with trace n − (1/n)·n = n − 1, so rank n − 1, and its nullity is 1 because it annihilates exactly the constant vectors. Verified at n = 4, 6 and 10.

C.why: True, because AᵀAx = 0 forces ‖Ax‖² = 0 and hence Ax = 0, so the two matrices have the same null space. This is why XᵀX is invertible exactly when X has full column rank.

D.why: False, with the two numbers swapped. The residual maker is idempotent with trace n − k, so its RANK is n − k and its nullity is k — it annihilates precisely the k-dimensional column space of X.

items.stem: For a real matrix A of order m × n, rank(AᵀA) is:
items.explanation: Equality holds because Ax = 0 and AᵀAx = 0 have the same solution set: if AᵀAx = 0 then xᵀAᵀAx = ‖Ax‖² = 0, forcing Ax = 0. So the two matrices have the same nullity and hence the same rank. This is why XᵀX is invertible exactly when X has full column rank.

items.stem: X is n × k of rank k. The nullity of P = I − X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is:
items.explanation: P is the residual maker: idempotent with trace n − k, so its rank is n − k and its nullity is n − (n − k) = k. Concretely it annihilates exactly the k-dimensional column space of X. Option A is its RANK, not its nullity — the commonest slip here.
items.check: Verified for a random 8 × 3 design of rank 3: rank(P) = 5 and nullity 3 = k.

items.stem: If υ(A) = 0 for a square matrix A, then A is:
items.explanation: Zero nullity means Ax = 0 only for x = 0, so the rank is full, the determinant is non-zero and the inverse exists. 'Non-singular' is the single word for all of those. Nothing follows about idempotence or symmetry.

items.stem: Consider rank and nullity of products of n × n matrices.
items.explanation: A is Sylvester's rank inequality. B is the nullity form, obtained from A by υ = n − rank. C is true and is why the Q1 interval cannot be sharpened. D is false: the bound is υ(A) + υ(B) with no subtraction, and A = B = I refutes the −n version.
statements: rank(A) + rank(B) − n ≤ rank(AB) ≤ min{rank(A), rank(B)}.
For 6 × 6 matrices with υ(A) = 3 and υ(B) = 2, both endpoints of the resulting interval [3, 5] are attainable.

A.why: True — Sylvester's rank inequality. The dimension subtracted is the shared one: the columns of A, equal to the rows of B.

B.why: True. Substituting υ = n − rank into A reverses both inequalities, turning min into max and rank A + rank B − n into υ(A) + υ(B). This is June 2026 Q1.

C.why: True, and verified by construction: A = diag(1,1,1,0,0,0) with B = diag(1,1,1,1,0,0) gives υ(AB) = 3, while a B whose image contains the whole null space of A gives υ(AB) = 5. Random examples find only the lower end, since subspaces in general position intersect minimally.

D.why: False. The correct bound has no −n. For A = B = I all three nullities are 0 and the claim reads 0 ≤ −n, which is absurd. This was the option marked in June 2026.

items.stem: Let A and B be 5 × 5 matrices with rank(A) = rank(B) = 3. The minimum possible value of rank(AB) is:
items.explanation: Sylvester's lower bound gives rank(AB) ≥ 3 + 3 − 5 = 1, and the bound is attained: take A = diag(1,1,1,0,0), whose null space is span{e₄, e₅}, and B with image span{e₁, e₄, e₅}. Then A destroys two of B's three image dimensions, leaving rank 1. Option D is the generic value, which is what random examples give.
items.check: A bound is only an answer if it is attainable, so construct an example rather than sampling — random integer matrices almost never reach the floor.

items.stem: Let A be a non-zero 3 × 3 matrix satisfying A² = 0. The maximum possible rank of A is:
items.explanation: A² = 0 means every column of A lies in the null space of A, so rank(A) ≤ υ(A) = 3 − rank(A), giving 2·rank(A) ≤ 3 and hence rank(A) ≤ 1. Since A is non-zero the rank is exactly 1, and such matrices exist — for example the matrix with a single 1 in the top-right corner.
items.check: The argument is rank ≤ nullity plus rank–nullity; it generalises to rank ≤ ⌊n/2⌋ for any n × n matrix with A² = 0.

items.stem: A regression is fitted with an intercept plus a full set of four indicator columns for four categories. The resulting difficulty is best described as:
options: the design matrix has nullity 1, so a one-parameter family of coefficients gives identical fits
the determinant of X is negative
items.explanation: The four indicators sum to the intercept column, so one of the five columns is a combination of the others: rank 4, nullity 1. Adding c to the intercept and subtracting c from every category effect leaves all fitted values unchanged, so the fit is unique while the coefficients are not. Since rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) = 4 < 5, XᵀX is singular and different software returns different members of the same family.
